text: Noninvasive sampling of DNA from larval exuvia in diving beetles of the genera Cybister and Dytiscus

Nonlethal DNA sampling is a highly recommendable method in molecular genetic studies of protected and endangered species. To develop a demonstrably nonlethal method of obtaining DNA from larvae of endangered diving beetles (Cybister brevis, C. lewisianus, C. limbatus, C. rugosus, Dytiscus sharpi sharpi and D. sharpi validus), we obtained the larval exuvia (molted skin) of these endangered diving beetles under laboratory conditions. A single exuvia 24 h after molting was sufficient to allow polymerase chain reaction (PCR) detection of a mitochondrial DNA gene, cytochrome-c oxidase subunit I (COI), and the sequence of the COI gene could be determined directly. Sequences obtained from the exuvial samples were used to further find similarities within DDBJ/EMBL/GenBank. Genomic DNA from the samples was successfully isolated, and we identified the species. This process suggests that exuvia provides a good sample for extracting DNA from endangered diving beetle larvae without killing them.

Nonlethal or noninvasive sampling for DNA analysis has become an important approach in conservation genetics studies, particularly for endangered and protected species (Vila et al. 2009). Nonlethal sampling methods are also applied to insects; in these methods DNA is usually extracted from a leg or wing (e.g. Keyghobadi et al. 1999;Lai & Pullin 2004;Vila et al. 2009;Hamm et al. 2010). Nonlethal sampling of DNA from diving beetles using a single antenna has also been reported (Suzuki et al. 2012). Lefort et al. (2012) reported noninvasive molecular methods to identify live scarab larvae using larval exuviae and frass as sources of DNA. Serjeant and Beebee (2013) reported that DNA was extracted from six Dytiscus diving beetle larvae found in Britain, and determined the partial sequence of the cytochrome-c oxidase subunit I (COI) gene to identify species. They used single amputated legs of the larvae for analysis because individuals in this condition are sometimes found in the wild and in the laboratory amputees seem to survive well. However, there have been no reports to date on the techniques of noninvasive sampling of DNA from larvae of aquatic beetles.
The habitats of freshwater species, including insects and other invertebrates, are increasingly threatened worldwide (Allan & Flecker 1993). Cybister lewisianus Sharp, C. limbatus (Fabricius), C. rugosus (MacLeay), Dytiscus sharpi sharpi Wehncke and Dytiscus sharpi validus Régimbart have been designated as critically endangered species in Japan, and most of them have also been designated as national endangered species of wild fauna and flora of Japan (Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan 2011, 2012). Cybister brevis Aubé is designated as a near-threatened species in Japan (Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan 2012). Adult aquatic insects, such as Cybister and Dytiscus species, are readily distinguished by a suite of characteristics including size, color and shape (e.g. Mori & Kitayama 2002). However, these larvae, specifically among Cybister or Dytiscus species, have very similar morphologies within the same genus. For appropriate conservation measurements, accurate identification is an essential prerequisite for surveying and monitoring populations. Although Kamite (2008) briefly described and keyed the third instar larvae of 21 species and one subspecies of the subfamily Dytiscinae, the keys all rely on small differences in features that are difficult to observe accurately in the field and thus require the larvae to be killed before observation. Furthermore, the keys were only based on the third instar larvae. Young beetle larvae, that is at the first instar stage, are very difficult to distinguish morphologically from one another. However, since younger larvae are generally more abundant than older larvae and adults, samples of younger larvae can be more easily obtained for such studies both in the field and in the laboratory.
In the present study, larval exuviae (first or second larval stages) of diving beetles were collected under breeding conditions. Furthermore, genomic DNA was extracted from a single exuvia that was preserved in pure ethanol for 3 to 4 months. These exuviae were derived from the following endangered species: C. brevis, C. lewisianus, C. limbatus, C. rugosus, D. sharpi sharpi and D. sharpi validus. In addition, the COI gene (725-776 bp region for Cybister, 628 bp for Dytiscus) was amplified by the standard polymerase chain reaction (PCR) method. We were able to carry out direct sequencing on the amplified COI gene to identify species.
The collection sites of the diving beetles are listed in Table 1. These insects were kept in aquaria according to methods described previously (Tsuzuki et al. 1999;Inoda & Kamimura 2004;Inoda & Kitano 2013) in order to obtain larval exuviae. The collection of C. lewisianus, C. limbatus, D. sharpi sharpi and D. sharpi validus is currently restricted by law (Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan 2011), but the samples analyzed here were taken before the law came into effect.
We collected the exuviae from first or second instar larvae within 24 h after molting. Usually the exuviae are floating just beneath the surface of the water, the tail end is up and the head is pointing downwards. The exuviae were taken from aquaria and immediately blotted to remove excess water. One to ten exuviae were stored in 15 mL of 95-99% ethanol. After a few days, the ethanol was changed and the exuviae were stored at room temperature until DNA extraction (at 3 to 4 months). Then, one exuvia of the first instar stage (second instar stage for D. sharpi validus) from each beetle larva was used for analysis. Total DNA was extracted using the HotSHOT method of Truett et al. (2000) with some modifications as follows. One exuvia was put into a microtube containing 100 μL of 50 mM NaOH. Then the tube was heated at 95°C for 10 min. The tube was put on ice and 10 μL of 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) was added. The tube was tapped and spun down at 17 800 × g, 4°C for 1 min. A part (5 μL) of the resultant supernatant was used for the PCR template.
The partial COI fragment was amplified by PCR using a set of primers: Jerry (5′-CAA CAT TTA TTT TGA TTT TTT GG-3′) and Pat (5′-TCC AAT GCA CTA ATC TGC CAT ATT A-3′), which were designed by Simon et al. (1994). The amplification mixture (50 μL) contained 5 μL of template DNA, 2 mM of a dNTP mixture (Toyobo, Osaka, Japan), 1 μL of KOD FX Neo (Toyobo) and 1.5 μM of each primer. The reactions were performed with a first denaturation step of 2 min at 94°C followed by 35 cycles of 10 s at 98°C, 30 s at 56°C and 1 min at 68°C in a thermal cycler (Veriti; Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). The final extension step of 2 min was performed at 68°C. The PCR product was subjected to electrophoresis. The gel was stained with ethidium bromide and imaged using a Gel Doc 2000 apparatus and Quantity One software (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA). The DNA content was measured by a photometer (NanoDrop ND-2000C; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The products were purified using a QIAquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer's instructions. After the cycle sequencing reaction was performed using DTCS QuickStart Master Mix (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA), the sequences  Although many scientists have reported noninvasive or nonlethal sampling of DNA from many insects, no data regarding the use of noninvasive methods in larvae of aquatic beetles have been reported to date. Suzuki et al. (2012) reported the use of a nonlethal sampling method of DNA in adult diving beetles. They used a single antenna for DNA analysis. However, the method can not be applied to diving beetle larvae because their bodies are too small and soft to be handled. Obtaining legs from small beetle larvae required a high skill level. Specifically, first instar larvae of C. brevis and C. lewisianus are not large enough (17-18 mm;Ichikawa 1984) to remove their delicate legs using the method described in Serjeant and Beebee (2013). We used the exuvia (molted skin) of the beetle larvae because exuvia is available when beetles grow to the next instar stage. The exuvia is useless to the beetle larvae, and easy to get. Takahashi et al. (2009) reported that molted skins of endangered dragonflies (Libellila angelina) were used for analysis of the genetic diversity and differentiation so that they will not affect the population size of the species. Since many diving beetles are also facing possible extinction (Ministry of the Environment, Government of Japan 2011, 2012), it is important to conduct research without damaging not only individual insects but also the population level, as in the study by Takahashi et al. (2009).
In the present study, the results suggest that the COI gene could be amplified from different species of larval exuvia in diving beetles as well as in ground beetles (Lefort et al. 2012). DNA sequences also obtained from exuviae were used to identify both Cybister and Dytiscus species. Although we have not yet applied this method to all of the Japanese specimens, larval exuvia could become a useful DNA source for the identification of species and for conducting other molecular studies. This noninvasive method will contribute to further molecular investigation of endangered diving beetles in the future.
